Triggers.value: Feeling physically restrained or held down

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

vignette: Two years ago, Amara lay on a concrete floor, her wrists zip-tied behind her and a heavy knee pressing her down. The man leaning over her breathed through his mouth, a heavy rhythm filling the small room. He wore a thick sandalwood cologne that clung to the air. Every time he inhaled, the sound grew louder, echoing the pressure holding her back. She remembered the peeling paint on the ceiling, but when she tried to hold the rest of the room in her mind, the details dissolved into static. The events of those days refused to settle into a coherent timeline. Some nights, she would sit at her desk to piece the years together, but her thoughts kept sliding away before she could grasp them. The fragments she managed to retrieve felt distant, like watching a documentary about a stranger. She knew there were months she had simply lost, as if the pages had been torn out. Over the following spring, she began taking different routes to the courthouse. She stopped using the basement parking garage entirely. When the deputy clerk wore a citrus cologne to the morning briefing, Amara excused herself to the restroom and stayed until the scent faded. She told herself it was merely a preference, though her shoulders tightened before she even entered the room. During a lengthy deposition, a bailiff’s heavy breathing filled the chamber. Amara’s grip tightened on the wooden bench. She began asking colleagues to handle the late-night case reviews, preferring to step out to the perimeter hallway instead. Her husband, David, would reach for her shoulder in the evenings, but she pulled back, her breath catching. She did not explain why. She simply moved to the other side of the bed. The distance between them widened quietly, measured in closed doors. Now, at the bench, the courtroom demanded a steadiness she no longer recognized. During a custody hearing, a young father’s heavy breathing filled the air as his attorney paced. Amara’s pen paused. She felt a sudden pull at her wrists, a weight pressing down her back. The air carried the faint scent of the court reporter’s cologne. She ordered a recess and pressed her palms against her office window. She had come to believe that sitting in the front row would overwhelm her, so she now presided from a remote gallery. Her colleagues noticed her retreat. What frightened her most was the quiet erosion of her own certainty. She scheduled this appointment hoping to reclaim the years she felt slipping away, though she doubted the missing pieces could ever be found. She sat on the edge of the therapist’s chair, waiting to see if speaking aloud would help, or if some things were simply meant to remain out of reach.
